headline: Economists Stunned: Tariffs Still Happening Despite Last-Minute Prayers
subheadline: With 12:01 a.m. Wednesday looming, dealmakers discover that strongly-worded statements do not, in fact, stop trade wars.
source_headline: Here's what top economists are saying about the potential impact of Trump's 50 per cent tariffs as deadline nears
body_html:
As the clock ticks toward 12:01 a.m. on Wednesday, Canadian and U.S. officials find themselves in that special purgatory where a 50 percent tariff is both imminent and somehow still theoretically preventable. Economists are now weighing in with their expert analysis—a polite euphemism for "saying things loudly while hoping someone important is listening." The deadline, we are told, is firm. Real. Inexorable. Which is why it has suddenly become the backdrop for what can only be described as financial theater of the absurd, where deal structures hang in limbo and M&A teams refresh their email every 90 seconds.

For those keeping score at home, a 50 percent tariff is not a negotiating position—it is a restructuring event masquerading as foreign trade policy. When duties double, supply chains don't just adjust; they atomize. Cross-border M&A becomes an exercise in retroactive valuation archaeology: "We bought this company at $500 million for its Canadian manufacturing footprint. It is now worth $240 million. Also, our accountants have started drinking directly from the bottle." The Canadian and U.S. officials tasked with preventing this have roughly 36 hours remaining. One can sense the vigorous optimism from here.

What makes this particular brand of deadline theater so rich is its refusal to learn from precedent. Trade tensions have become a recurring feature of the dealmaking calendar, like earnings season but with tariffs. Each time, executives insist this time is different. This time, cooler heads will prevail. This time, nobody is actually insane enough to trigger a 50 percent duty. And yet, here we are, hours away from discovering whether cooler heads have, in fact, vacated the premises entirely.

Top economists, bless them, are now "saying things about the potential impact." Translation: they are describing in measured, peer-reviewed language what private equity analysts have already priced in via midnight spreadsheets and self-medicated panic. The tariffs will affect supply chains. Export-dependent sectors will face headwinds. Cross-border valuations will require revision. None of this is remotely surprising to anyone whose job depends on understanding how tariffs work. What is surprising is that we keep pretending each fresh deadline represents a genuine possibility of avoidance rather than theater's final curtain call.

The real question lurking beneath the deadline is what happens to the $300 billion in pending cross-border M&A deals currently trapped in diligence. Do valuations reset? Do earnouts shift to tariff-hedged structures? Do we simply accept that the entire integrated North American supply chain is now a speculative asset class? Private equity thrives on information asymmetry and timing arbitrage. A 50 percent tariff imposed at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday is neither—it is a sledgehammer, and sledgehammers are bad for premium multiples.

The tariff deadline is now less than 36 hours away. Canadian and U.S. officials remain in active negotiation, which is diplomatic language for "desperately hoping the other side blinks first." Economists continue to issue carefully-worded statements about potential impacts. And in conference rooms from Toronto to New York, dealmakers are doing what they do best: assuming that reality will conform to their spreadsheet rather than vice versa. It is a beautiful delusion. History suggests it will not age well.

When the clock strikes 12:01 a.m. Wednesday, we will discover whether last-minute diplomacy was theater or salvation. Spoiler alert: it was theater. Tariffs do not negotiate. They simply activate. And then the real work begins—repricing an entire continent's worth of M&A at tariff-adjusted multiples. Economists will publish papers about this. Private equity will take the losses. And in 18 months, we will do this again.
glossary_definition: A valuation metric that exists only in PowerPoint presentations and represents what a company would theoretically be worth if we all agreed to ignore the tariff that just destroyed its margins.
